topic: British Economic and Administrative Policies (Indian History)
description: The economic and administrative policies of the British East India Company and the British Crown profoundly impacted the Indian economy and governance. The primary objective of these policies was the economic exploitation of India and the expansion of the British Empire.

sections.title: Land Revenue Systems
sections.description: The major land tax systems implemented in India during the British period.

key_concepts.explanation: Under this system, Zamindars were recognized as the permanent owners of the land. The revenue amount was fixed, with 10/11th going to the British government and 1/11th retained by the Zamindar.
A direct settlement made between the government and the cultivators (Ryots). The cultivator was recognized as the owner of the land and paid taxes directly to the government.
The revenue was assessed on the basis of a village or 'Mahal' as a whole. The village headman was responsible for collecting the tax and paying it to the government.

key_associations.extra_info: Introduced in 1793 in Bengal, Bihar, and Odisha.
Introduced in 1820 in parts of Madras, Bombay, and Assam.
Introduced in 1822 in the North-Western Provinces, Punjab, and Central Provinces.

sections.title: Economic Impact
sections.description: The decline and exploitation of the Indian economy under British rule.

key_concepts.explanation: This theory explains how India's wealth and resources were being systematically transferred to Britain without any adequate economic return (e.g., in the form of salaries, pensions, and profits).
The ruin of traditional Indian handicrafts and cottage industries due to the influx of cheap machine-made goods imported from British factories.
Peasants were forced to grow cash crops like indigo, cotton, and opium instead of food crops, which heavily contributed to severe famines.

key_associations.item: Poverty and Un-British Rule in India
key_associations.extra_info: This book provided the first detailed economic critique of British imperialism and elaborated on the 'Drain of Wealth' theory.
A seminal work that strongly criticized British economic policies and their devastating effect on the Indian peasantry.

sections.title: Expansionist and Annexation Policies
sections.description: Diplomatic and administrative strategies used to annex Indian princely states into the British Empire.

key_concepts.explanation: The policy of defending the company's frontiers by treating neighboring states as buffer zones to absorb any external shocks.
A treaty in which an Indian ruler had to disband their own army, maintain a British contingent, and station a British Resident at their court.

According to this policy, if an Indian ruler died without a natural male heir, their state would automatically be annexed by the British Empire. Adopted sons were not recognized as legitimate heirs to the throne.

key_associations.extra_info: Mainly implemented with Awadh to create a buffer against the Marathas and Afghans.
The Nizam of Hyderabad was the first Indian ruler to accept this alliance in 1798.
States annexed under this doctrine include Satara (1848), Jhansi (1853), and Nagpur (1854).

sections.title: Administrative and Judicial Reforms
sections.description: The evolution of the civil services, judiciary, and local administration in British India.

historical_events.significance: A Supreme Court was established at Calcutta, with Sir Elijah Impey serving as its first Chief Justice.
Introduced an open competitive examination system for the recruitment of Civil Servants (based on the Macaulay Committee recommendations).

important_facts.fact: Lord Cornwallis is widely regarded as the 'Father of Civil Services in India' for reforming and organizing the administrative machinery.
In 1863, Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian to successfully clear the Indian Civil Service (ICS) examination.
Lord Ripon is celebrated as the 'Father of Local Self-Government in India' for his resolution of 1882.
During the tenure of Lord William Bentinck, English was made the official medium of higher education based on Macaulay's Minute of 1835.
